Redwood owners: Jordan Lee, Priya Patel, Luis Moreno

Recording: yes
Notes: Weekly POC sync for latency tuning (TTFT, streaming, seq length, kernel choices)
summary: Weekly check-in focused on reducing time-to-first-token (TTFT) and tail latency. Reviewed profiling results from last week, agreed on kernel-level profiling by sequence length, will test streaming in staging, and adjust batching/kv-cache settings. Action items assigned for next week; Jordan to follow up with pricing and Dedicated node options.
topics: Sequence length distribution and kernel selection
transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Lee: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call then we'll jump in.
[00:08] Samantha Ortiz: Hi all, Samantha here.
[00:10] Evan Cole: Evan — ML eng.
[00:12] Maya Gupta: Maya — SRE.
[00:14] Priya Patel: Priya from Redwood. Luis is on as well.
[00:18] Jordan Lee: Cool. Last week we shipped the new kernel build and a couple of profiling runs. Priya, you wanna kick off with the results?
[00:27] Priya Patel: Sure. So we ran the kernel profiler across your three main seq length buckets — short ~32 tokens, mid ~128, and long ~512. The headline: TTFT improvements are most visible on short sequences with the new fused-attn kernel, we saw median TTFT drop from ~210ms to ~160ms on the 32-token workload.
[00:45] Priya Patel: For mid sequences the gains are smaller, about 10-15%; for 512 we're hitting memory-bandwidth limits and the kernel choice matters a lot — certain matmul tiling helps but tail latency at p99 didn't improve much.
[01:05] Evan Cole: Quick q — when you say TTFT are you including network overhead? Our staging tests include our ingress LB which adds ~30-40ms.
[01:15] Priya Patel: Good point. The profiler numbers are server-side only. When we run end-to-end with your LB we add that 30-40ms; so end-to-end TTFT for short sequences in staging was about 200ms.
[01:28] Samantha Ortiz: Our goal is sub-200ms average TTFT for the common quick-query path. Is that realistic without going to Dedicated?
[01:36] Jordan Lee: Possibly. We have a couple levers: enable streaming to get first token out earlier, smaller batch sizes for lower tail, and kernel selection tuned to your sequence mix. Dedicated nodes definitely reduce noisy neighbors but aren't always required.
[01:50] Maya Gupta: Streaming worries me — we've seen cases where streaming increases p95/p99 because it keeps the connection open and limits batching. Any thoughts?
[01:59] Priya Patel: Yeah, streaming trades off throughput for faster TTFT. In our internal runs, enabling streaming cut TTFT by ~40-60ms for 32-token requests, but p95 went up slightly because batching opportunities reduced. For your traffic mix (80% short queries), streaming could be net-positive, but we need to validate in staging.
[02:20] Evan Cole: If we enable streaming, can we still use the KV cache to preserve context?
[02:24] Priya Patel: Absolute yes — kv cache works with streaming. We just need to ensure the runtime maintains an efficient cache lookup path; some older kernels had cache-copy overhead. The new build reduces that.
[02:35] Jordan Lee: Luis, you had the bench spreadsheet up?
[02:38] Luis Moreno: Yep. Sharing link in chat — drive.google.com/xxx (redacted). The sheet has per-kernel, per-seq-length TTFT, latency percentiles, and GPU utilization.
[02:48] Luis Moreno: Notably, the int8 quantized path lowers token cost by ~40% but adds ~5-12ms to TTFT on short sequences due to dequantize steps — so cost vs latency trade-off.
[03:02] Samantha Ortiz: So quantization helps cost but may hurt our TTFT targets, that's a bummer.
[03:08] Priya Patel: Right, it's workload dependent. For batch-oriented long responses it's great. For low-latency short queries, staying fp16 on the hot path might be better. Also kernel choice matters: the fused kernels for attention give you both speed and reduced memory ops, which helps TTFT without quantization.
[03:27] Evan Cole: About the kernel selection — can the runtime auto-select based on sequence length at request time? We have mixed requests in a single endpoint.
[03:36] Priya Patel: Yes, runtime can route to different execution paths per-request. There's a small routing overhead — ~2-4ms — but net win overall. We can also split your traffic into two routes if you want to optimize aggressively.
[03:46] Maya Gupta: What's the impact on GPU utilization if we route small sequences to a different kernel?
[03:50] Priya Patel: You'll likely see higher small-op efficiency and slightly lower utilization overall because small sequences have less compute per request, but latency improves. If utilization drops too much, we can suggest batching heuristics or a small Dedicated pool sized for short queries.
[04:05] Jordan Lee: Can we talk TTFT measurement methodology — Evan, you were going to run staged tests with actual LB in front?
[04:12] Evan Cole: Yes, I'm spinning up a run that mimics production ingress and will capture TTFT, T50/95/99 with streaming toggled. Plan to run with 1k requests to get signal.
[04:21] Priya Patel: Please include cold-start scenarios; even with warm pools we see cold KV cache misses on some traffic patterns and TTFT spikes.
[04:28] Evan Cole: Will do.
[04:30] Samantha Ortiz: Another question: how does Dedicated vs Hosted affect tail latency under noisy tenants?
[04:36] Jordan Lee: Dedicated gives you isolation and predictable p99s. Hosted can be fine if you tune autoscaling and use instance pinning, but you may see higher variance under very spiky traffic.
[04:47] Priya Patel: Also worth noting: fallback policies — if a high-capacity node is under pressure we can route to a lower-capacity but faster small-seq kernel variant to keep TTFT acceptable, that's part of the smart routing we mentioned earlier.
[04:57] Oliver Tan: Any security or compliance blockers if we test Dedicated?
[05:01] Jordan Lee: No blockers — Dedicated includes VPC options and KMS support. We'll send the security checklist.
[05:06] Maya Gupta: Please attach SOC2 docs again — our security team is still reviewing.
[05:09] Jordan Lee: For sure. I'll push the pack after the call.
[05:12] Priya Patel: Back to micro-optimizations: we found that setting max_sequence to 256 for short-route avoids extra kernel path and reduces p99 by ~15ms for those requests. It's a small config change.
[05:26] Priya Patel: Also we can adjust continuous batching window — lowering it from 60ms to 30ms reduces TTFT for low-concurrency bursts, but at the cost of throughput.
[05:40] Evan Cole: That seems promising. Our traffic has diurnal peaks but a lot of short spikes. Could be worth lowering window.
[05:49] Samantha Ortiz: Would lowering batching window increase cost significantly?
[05:53] Priya Patel: Somewhat — you lose batching efficiency so tokens/unit increases. We can model that in the spreadsheet; Jordan will include cost delta in the follow-up.
[06:05] Evan Cole: On telemetry, what should we instrument to validate TTFT improvements?
[06:09] Priya Patel: Capture ingress-to-first-byte, server-side scheduling delay, kernel execution time, kv-cache hit rate, and batch formation latency. Ideally include GPU utilization and mem bandwidth for long sequence runs.
[06:21] Maya Gupta: We'll add those metrics to our staging dashboards.
[06:24] Jordan Lee: Ok next, any blockers on tests this week?
[06:28] Evan Cole: I need the updated runtime build with fused-attn — the one you shared last week had a small bug on our infra; Priya you fixed and uploaded?
[06:35] Priya Patel: Fixed and uploaded yesterday under the bench folder. Link in chat. Should be the one with tag rwd-kernel-2026-08-30.
[06:42] Evan Cole: Got it, will pull.
[06:44] Samantha Ortiz: For acceptance criteria — our bar is average TTFT <200ms and p95 <350ms for the short-query cohort. Can we agree to aim for that by next checkpoint?
[06:55] Jordan Lee: Yes, that's reasonable. We'll focus on streaming + kernel selection + batching window adjustments. If we see regressions, we'll consider a small Dedicated pool.
[07:05] Priya Patel: Also want to run a quick sensitivity test on quantization — int8 impacts TTFT slightly but might be ok if our latency window holds; we'll include that in the profiling.
[07:18] Oliver Tan: Question on rollback: if streaming causes regressions in tail, how quick is rollback?
[07:23] Luis Moreno: Rollout is canary first then 10/30/100, and can be rolled back in under 5 minutes typically. We keep the previous model pinned until canary looks good.
[07:34] Maya Gupta: Good.
[07:36] Jordan Lee: Let's recap action items — Priya to share kernel-by-seq-length sheet; Evan to run streaming staging test; Maya to send prod p99s; Jordan to send pricing and dedicated proposal.
[07:50] Samantha Ortiz: Sounds good. Also please include a short note on expected cost delta for lowering batching window vs moving to Dedicated.
[07:56] Jordan Lee: Will do.
[08:00] Evan Cole: One more technical note — our typical max client-side seq length is 64 but with context we sometimes hit 256. If we can auto-route 64s to the fused kernel path we might hit target without big cost.
[08:12] Priya Patel: Yep that auto-routing is straightforward. We'll add routing rule suggestions in the sheet.
[08:20] Jordan Lee: Great. If nothing else, we'll reconvene same time next week. Thanks everyone.
[08:26] Samantha Ortiz: Thanks all.
[08:28] Jordan Lee: End of call.
